quotes.text: If you're a small business owner, you have to advertise more. Period. No one knows you exist - which is why you're not making as much as you want.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex responds to small business owners who assume customers will find them without consistent outbound marketing.

quotes.text: Always making things happen faster. Always disappointed it didn't happen faster.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex's reply in a conversation about founders who create urgency by being aggressive about pace.

quotes.text: Ambition without action is entitlement.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex draws a hard line between wanting something and actually working toward it.

quotes.text: The fastest way to change your life is to change where you invest: Look at your calendar for where you spend your time. Your credit card statement for how you spend your money. And your phone for where you spend your attention. Change your inputs. Change your outputs.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex turns personal change into an audit of the three resources people continuously allocate: time, money, and attention.

quotes.text: When your friends start to say “you’ve changed” - remember it’s because they don’t know how to say “you’ve grown.”
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex reframes a common criticism from friends as a description of growth rather than of betrayal.

quotes.text: Success is hard because it requires consistency not complexity.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex reframes why success is difficult: the hard part is repeating simple actions, not finding a more complicated method.

quotes.text: And so, one of my internal, uh, jokes that I have is the undefeated heavyweight champion of the world is do nothing.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins
quotes.context: Alex is comparing proposed actions with the option to keep resources on work that is already producing the highest return.
quotes.shortVersion: …the undefeated heavyweight champion of the world is do nothing.

quotes.text: You might have suggested it because you are emotionally uncomfortable with your existing moment and just want something to do rather than the thing that you know is going to work.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins
quotes.context: Alex warns that a new initiative can be an emotional escape from patiently continuing the proven course of action.

quotes.text: People only feel sold to if it's bad.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: If You Hate Selling, Please Watch This | Scale or Fail Episode 3
quotes.context: Alex responds to a founder who worries that a more structured webinar will make customers feel sold to.

quotes.text: You can’t fit in and also be exceptional. Both have discomfort. When you fit in, you have internal conflict because you’re not being 100% you. When you’re exceptional, you have external conflict because everyone sees you as different. Pick.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex lays out the tradeoff between belonging and standing out, and argues that both choices carry a cost.
quotes.shortVersion: You can’t fit in and also be exceptional…

quotes.text: The reason focus is so important in the beginning is that the only solid employee in your business is you. And you would never tell that person to work on four things at the same time and see what works.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex compares an early-stage founder splitting attention across projects to mismanaging their only reliable employee: themselves.

quotes.text: Hard times feel long. But an epic story lasts a lifetime.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex offers a reframe for enduring difficulty: the story you will tell later outlasts how long the hardship feels right now.

quotes.text: People don’t have shorter attention spans, they have higher standards and better alternatives.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex pushes back on the idea that audiences cannot focus, arguing what actually changed is what audiences will tolerate.

quotes.text: And so, a lot of lack of focus is actually intellectual laziness.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins
quotes.context: Alex explains that people often retreat to familiar work when they encounter a problem they do not yet know how to solve.

quotes.text: Best way to learn sales without selling: Listen to close call recordings. The real world teaches more than any script.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex recommends studying real sales calls as a practical way to build sales judgment before taking calls yourself.

quotes.text: Don’t expect mediocre people to support world class goals.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex warns that people who have not pursued a demanding goal themselves often will not encourage one.

quotes.text: 5 reasons your offer isn't converting: 1) Targeting poor people 2) Not enough Proof 3) Too little friction 4) Big outcome not fast enough 5) "Sounds like work"
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex lists the most common reasons a sales offer fails to convert.

quotes.text: That’s the thing about opportunity. It looks like risk when it’s an opportunity. And by the time it’s risk free, it’s not an opportunity anymore.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex explains why meaningful opportunities cannot be separated from uncertainty: certainty usually arrives only after the upside has disappeared.

quotes.text: You don’t become confident by shouting affirmations in the mirror, but by having a stack of undeniable proof that you are who you say you are. Outwork your self doubt.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex argues confidence is built from an accumulated record of your own work rather than from self-talk.

quotes.text: Productivity comes from all the things you choose not to do.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex ties productivity to elimination rather than to doing more.

quotes.text: And every one of those purchases, somebody for sure thought about how to get you to buy.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: If You Hate Selling, Please Watch This | Scale or Fail Episode 3
quotes.context: Alex points out that good selling can feel natural even though someone intentionally designed the purchase journey.

quotes.text: Regrets come when we imagine an upside we didn’t experience without factoring in the cost we would’ve had to pay to get it.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex describes regret as an incomplete comparison that counts a missed benefit while ignoring the price required to obtain it.

quotes.text: You have a responsibility to the business. And the business has a responsibility to customers. But your responsibility is to make sure the business survives and grows.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: If You Hate Selling, Please Watch This | Scale or Fail Episode 3
quotes.context: Alex explains why a founder must price and structure delivery so the company can continue serving customers.

quotes.text: And if your business includes none, that's okay, work at retention first, and then backfill the rest.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)
quotes.context: After reviewing five business-model advantages, Alex recommends improving retention before the remaining advantages.

quotes.text: If you do not have what's called revenue retention, you have nothing.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)
quotes.context: Alex introduces revenue retention as the first and most important advantage of a strong business model.

quotes.text: The biggest reason the rich get richer (besides compounding) is they avoid things that don't make enough money. The more money you have, the more selective you are about which things are worth doing because fewer things move the needle for you.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: The opening of a longer thread where Alex explains that wealthier people get richer partly because they are more selective about which opportunities are even worth their time.

quotes.text: Best reason to take risk when you're poor: If you "have nothing left" it also means you have "nothing to lose." Giving you no reason not to take your shot.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex reframes having nothing left as having nothing to lose, removing the excuse not to act.

quotes.text: Cold calling and high volume selling are valuable because of the skills you learn, not the $. It’s hard to take 20+ consults a day and not get good. And once you’re good, it’s like getting a permanent $200k/yr pay raise. It’s worth giving a year to gain the skill for life.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex argues that the durable value of high-volume selling is the lifelong skill built through repeated real-world practice.

quotes.text: The biggest lie I believed for the first 10yrs of being a business owner was that scaling was about getting more customers. It's about getting customers to never leave. Scaling looks like a flat retention curve, and when your business never gets smaller, it scales by default.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex reframes scaling as keeping customers long enough for the business to stop shrinking, rather than treating acquisition alone as growth.

quotes.text: The easiest way to reduce churn is to sell stuff people already don’t cancel out of. TLDR: you’re never gonna make a gym membership stickier than Internet service across a large population.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex argues that retention is partly structural: some categories naturally support more durable customer relationships than others.

quotes.text: We don’t rise to the standards we have when others are watching we fall to the standards we have when no one is.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex describes standards as what you hold to privately, not what you perform when an audience is present.

quotes.text: If you’re gonna do it next year, you might as well start now and start enjoying the benefits sooner. And if the benefits aren’t good enough to do it now, they’re not gonna be any better in the future. So either change the goal or change yourself.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex challenges delayed goals by asking whether the promised benefit is meaningful enough to justify beginning now.

quotes.text: The reason you are stressed is you have decisions to make and you're not making them.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Post on X (@AlexHormozi)
quotes.context: Alex locates the source of stress in unresolved decisions rather than in the decisions themselves.

quotes.text: But if you're in an industry that has no retention, then switching to one that does, if you're early in your career, may not be the dumbest decision.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)
quotes.context: Alex qualifies the advice for people early in their careers whose current industry structurally lacks repeat purchasing.

quotes.text: Doing more is capped by time and physical ability. How much you get—a.k.a. leverage—is uncapped.

quotes.context: Alex uses this idea to reframe the discomfort and discipline involved in meaningful progress.

quotes.text: If you want to move fast, improve constantly and be surrounded by people who make you better, then sincere candor is the standard.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: What Leila Hormozi And I Accomplished In Q1 And HOW We Did It | Ep 835

quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Stop Trying to Get Rich. Get Better | Ep 714
quotes.context: Alex connects this idea to delivering value customers can feel and continue paying for.

quotes.text: And so, I almost always wrap my questions with "What would it take?" because it assumes success.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins
quotes.context: Alex contrasts this framing with asking whether something can be done; the former starts from an assumption that a solution exists.

quotes.text: The person who has the most context on you is you.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex argues that personal decisions should weigh one's own complete context more heavily than partial outside opinions.

quotes.text: You will live an imperfect life. Period.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex presents imperfection as the unavoidable result of finite time and competing priorities.

quotes.text: The goal of youth is optionality and the goal of adulthood is commitment.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex contrasts preserving possibilities early in life with deliberately eliminating alternatives through adult commitments.

quotes.text: Being cringe is the tax you pay when you start to prove to the world that you care more about what you want than how you look.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex argues that visible earnestness is a necessary cost of prioritizing a meaningful goal over appearances.

quotes.text: You finish what you started.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex emphasizes completion as the standard for honoring a commitment.

quotes.text: Right now, everyone who’s listening to this, you have accomplished things that you said would make you happy.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex asks listeners to notice that achievements once expected to create happiness may already be present.

quotes.text: If you like the priorities that you have, then you won.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex defines success as genuinely valuing the priorities reflected by one's actual life.

quotes.text: You have to make the call. You have to make the decision.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex emphasizes that progress requires choosing rather than continuing to preserve every alternative.

quotes.text: Today, you do the only thing you can do. You fight.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex describes action and resistance as the response available when circumstances are difficult.

quotes.text: The larger game is trying to win at life and realizing that each of these are components of it.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex places individual life categories inside the broader objective of building a satisfying life overall.

quotes.text: Stand tall. Don’t crack. Endure.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex opens with a challenge to remain steady and courageous under pressure.

quotes.text: You rage on.

quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex delivers a short imperative to continue with intensity through adversity.

quotes.text: I’m willing to give up these other things for the things that I care about most.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex frames intentional living as willingly sacrificing lower priorities for what matters most.

quotes.text: Be more dangerous than the forces that hope to destroy you.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex frames resilience as developing greater strength than the opposition or pressure one faces.

quotes.text: They sit passively by and let options expire.

quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex warns that refusing to choose still produces an outcome as available options expire.

quotes.text: A lot of the best things in life come on the other side of commitments.

quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex argues that many valuable outcomes only become available after a person commits.

quotes.text: There’s only one because only one thing can come first.

quotes.context: Alex explains why a true priority is singular: only one thing can occupy the first position.

quotes.text: Options only have value when they are exercised.

quotes.text: Whatever you don’t have is what you want.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex summarizes how attention shifts toward the benefits of whichever life choice was not made.

quotes.text: Whenever you invest in any of those 10 things, you pull away from others.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex explains that time invested in one life priority necessarily reduces the time available to another.

quotes.text: Make reality your today.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex gives a compact call to turn an intended future into present action.

quotes.text: You have to cut off one future.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex describes decision-making as selecting one path by closing off another possible future.

quotes.text: What box am I living in that I’m unaware of that has invisible walls that is keeping me in?
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex uses a reflective question to uncover unspoken rules and assumptions that constrain action.

quotes.text: Some games that even if you’re just playing them, you beat everyone else because the game that you’re optimizing for is just a superior game.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex explains that choosing a superior objective can create an advantage before execution quality is compared.

quotes.text: No matter how much it costs, how long it takes, or how much it hurts because you said you would.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex frames endurance as keeping a promise even when the cost, duration, or discomfort increases.

quotes.text: The constant source of dissatisfaction is me.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex identifies his own recurring desire for alternatives as the stable source of dissatisfaction.

quotes.text: At some point, you have to pull the trigger.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex says optionality must eventually give way to a concrete decision.

quotes.text: You do what you came to do.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex urges the listener to stay aligned with the purpose that brought them to the work.

quotes.text: If you do not have courage, nothing else matters.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex presents courage as the prerequisite for making any other strength useful.

quotes.text: You must make trades. You have to make a trade.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex states that meaningful prioritization always requires accepting a trade-off.

quotes.text: We always want what we can’t have.
quotes.author: Alex Hormozi
quotes.sourceTitle: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.
quotes.context: Alex describes the recurring human tendency to desire whichever alternative is unavailable.
